## The Secret Code of the Bells: How Every Toll is Deciphered

The tolling of a bell was never a random sound. Every strike, every pause, and every rhythmic sequence responded to a precise code that the locals learned from childhood without the need for manuals or formal explanations. In Almuñécar, as in so many towns across the Spanish landscape, the bell tower functioned as a communications center where bronze substituted for the spoken word. It took only a few seconds of listening to know if someone had died, if fire threatened the threshing floors, or if the procession was already turning the corner of the square.

The most revealing case of this system is the toll for the dead, traditionally known as the *clamor*. The elder bell ringers of Almuñécar describe a slow, rope-rung execution, where two bells alternate in a deep, spaced-out dialogue that seems to imitate the community's contained weeping. The key lay not only in the cadence but also in the number of strikes: in Almuñécar, two tolls announced the death of a woman, three that of a man, although these codes varied notably from region to region. This seemingly minor detail allowed the locals to immediately identify the sex of the deceased before the news spread through the streets.

The precision of the code left no room for ambiguity. A bell ringer who miscounted the number of tolls could sow confusion throughout the town, attributing the loss to the wrong family or generating unnecessary alarm. For this reason, the craft demanded absolute concentration and a profound knowledge of local variations, passed down from master to apprentice over years of practice in the bell tower. The elders of Almuñécar still remember how their grandparents would halt any conversation upon hearing the first toll of the *clamor*, mentally counting the strikes to decipher the message.

In contrast to the solemnity of the toll for the dead, the festive peals unleashed a completely different energy. The rhythms accelerated until they became almost frenetic, with the bells spinning at high speed and the clappers striking the bronze in uninterrupted cascades. No two festivals were alike: the patron saint's day, Corpus Christi, or the arrival of the bishop each had their own characteristic sequence, recognizable even from the most distant orchards on the outskirts of town. The bell ringer became a sort of folk musician, interpreting centuries-old scores with no other instrument than the rope and the counterweight.

Alarm tolls occupied a place apart in this sonic vocabulary. They were repetitive, intense peals, devoid of the rhythmic grace of celebrations or the meditative pause of funerals. Their function was purely practical: to mobilize the locals in the event of a fire, a flood, or any collective threat demanding an immediate response. In an era without sirens or public address systems, the bell tower was the only loudspeaker capable of waking an entire town in the dead of night or summoning the men from the fields in a matter of minutes.

Processions, for their part, required an accompanying toll that marked the route of the brotherhoods through the streets. This was neither a festive peal nor an alarm, but a steady pulse that guided the pace of the bearers and announced to the sick, who could not leave their homes, the exact moment the image was passing by their door. The bell ringers of Almuñécar adjusted the intensity according to the distance: softer when the procession was far away, more powerful as it approached the church, creating a sonic geography that the locals interpreted effortlessly.

This system functioned as an authentic "WhatsApp of the past," according to an expression popularized by recent ethnography. The comparison is not exaggerated: the bells transmitted information in real time, without the need for the recipient to move or for a complex technological infrastructure to exist. A farmer working in his plot could know, simply by looking up and listening, whether he needed to return to town for an emergency or if he could continue his day without worry. Information traveled at the speed of sound, with an efficacy that is hard to imagine today.

The coding was not limited to major events. There were tolls for the Angelus, which structured the working day into three moments of prayer; tolls to call the council, which summoned the locals to the square to discuss communal affairs; and storm tolls, intended to ward off the storms that threatened the harvests. Each had its own rhythm, duration, and intensity, forming a vocabulary of dozens of distinct messages that any adult local mastered naturally. The bell tower was, ultimately, the nerve center of community life.

Today, when automation has replaced the human hand and the tolls are programmed via electronic systems, that vocabulary is vanishing at an alarming rate. The elder bell ringers of Almuñécar keep the keys to a language in their memory that almost no one else knows how to interpret, and with them disappears a way of understanding the community based on attentive listening and shared knowledge. The code of the bells, documented in Almuñécar since the mid-16th century, is slowly fading out without contemporary society having found a substitute that transmits as much information with so few resources.
